cases.holding: The Utah Supreme Court affirmed the court of appeals' disavowal of the 'almost automatically' line of cases and held that the statutory 'strictly necessary' requirement is not a separate third element but a mandatory part of the best-interest inquiry, so a juvenile court must expressly consider feasible alternatives to termination.
cases.quote: as part of that inquiry, a court must specifically address whether termination is strictly necessary to promote the child's welfare and best interest

relevance.OUT-02: This is the controlling Utah framework for terminating parental rights: grounds alone never suffice, and the court must find termination strictly necessary from the child's point of view.
relevance.OUT-03: Because termination is not strictly necessary where a permanent guardianship would equally protect the child, this case is the gateway authority for guardianship as a permanency alternative.
relevance.ACT-03: The opinion ties the strictly-necessary analysis to whether the child's out-of-home placement can be made permanent by a means short of severing the parent-child tie.
relevance.ACT-04: The Court highlights the statutory command that efforts to place the child with willing kin be given due weight before termination is found strictly necessary.

cases.holding: The Court reversed the court of appeals, holding that In re B.T.B. created no new substantive right, that appellate courts may not graft a 'materially better' test onto the statutory strictly-necessary standard, and that the court of appeals exceeded appropriate appellate review by reweighing evidence.
cases.quote: the court erred by applying the "materially better" standard instead of the relevant statutory language

relevance.OUT-02: It fixes the current Utah formulation of the strictly-necessary/best-interest test and rejects judicially added glosses on the statute.
relevance.FAIL-01: It marks the outer limit of appellate reversal of a juvenile court: an appellate court may not reweigh evidence or consider matter outside the record.

cases.holding: The Court reversed the court of appeals and reinstated the termination order, holding that the juvenile court's best-interest determination — including its rejection of permanent guardianship with the grandmother in favor of adoption — was supported by the evidence and not against its clear weight.
cases.quote: Because the juvenile court's best interest determination was supported by the evidence, we reverse.

relevance.OUT-02: It is the most recent Utah Supreme Court application of the strictly-necessary standard and confirms the deference owed to a juvenile court's termination decision.
relevance.OUT-03: The majority and dissent squarely debate when permanent guardianship is an adequate alternative to termination, making it the leading recent authority on that choice.

cases.holding: The Court held that the deferential State ex rel. B.R. standard of review applies to a juvenile court's best-interest determination, declined to replace it with de novo review, and clarified that the standard is the ordinary deference owed any fact-intensive lower-court decision.
cases.quote: we hold that the court of appeals correctly applied the B.R. standard of review to the juvenile court's best interest determination

relevance.FAIL-01: It states the standard an appellate court must use before it may reverse a juvenile court, and is therefore the measuring stick for every claimed court reversal of an agency-driven decision.

cases.holding: The Court declined to raise the burden of proof for termination from clear and convincing evidence to beyond a reasonable doubt, and held the juvenile court adequately conducted the strictly-necessary analysis, including considering the grandmother as a kinship alternative.
cases.quote: The juvenile court did not err in declining to apply the "beyond a reasonable doubt" standard of proof.

relevance.OUT-02: It settles that clear and convincing evidence, not proof beyond a reasonable doubt, is the Utah standard for terminating parental rights.
relevance.ACT-04: The Court's review of the juvenile court's treatment of the grandmother placement shows how kinship options must be weighed before termination.

cases.holding: The Court retained deferential review of best-interest determinations but vacated in part because the juvenile court committed threshold legal errors in assessing whether the father had made sufficient progress in rehabilitation under the reunification statute.
cases.quote: we reject the father's request that we abandon a deferential standard of review of a best interest determination

relevance.OUT-01: It holds that a juvenile court must correctly assess a parent's statutory progress toward rehabilitation before it can lawfully conclude that reunification should give way to termination.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed the court of appeals' reversal of a neglect adjudication, holding that nondeferential review was appropriate for the law-like mixed question and that the juvenile court's findings did not satisfy the statutory definition of neglect (or of abuse as an alternative ground).
cases.quote: the juvenile court's factual findings do not support any of the statutory grounds for neglect

relevance.DEC-03: It shows that an abuse or neglect finding must be tethered to the statutory definition; conduct a court finds troubling is not automatically 'neglect.'
relevance.DEC-05: A petition must plead and prove facts that fit the statutory grounds, or the adjudication cannot stand.
relevance.OUT-05: The case is the model for dismissal: findings that fail to meet the statutory definition require the adjudication to be set aside.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a Utah Supreme Court example of an appellate court correctly reversing a juvenile court's adjudication for legal insufficiency.

cases.holding: The Court held that the appeal period ran from entry of the termination order rather than from later-entered minutes, but that the mother's notice of appeal was nonetheless timely under Rule 52(c), and remanded for the court of appeals to reach the merits.
cases.quote: The court of appeals correctly ruled that the time for Mother to file her appeal ran from the entry of the Termination Order and not the subsequent Minutes.

relevance.FAIL-01: It governs when the short child-welfare appeal clock starts, which determines whether an erroneous juvenile court decision can be reviewed at all.
relevance.OUT-05: It shows that a later ministerial entry does not reopen finality, so parties must treat the substantive order as the operative closing event.

cases.holding: The Court reversed the court of appeals, holding that using the heightened clear-and-convincing standard at a permanency hearing is permissible and does not predetermine termination, and that the appellate court had improperly substituted its judgment for the juvenile court's.
cases.quote: When a foundation for the court's decision exists in the evidence, an appellate court may not engage in a reweighing of the evidence.

relevance.OUT-01: It explains that the permanency hearing asks only whether the child may safely be returned home, and that findings there do not dictate the later termination outcome.

cases.holding: The Court held that Title II of the ADA applies to the provision of reunification services under Utah's child welfare statutes, but affirmed because the juvenile court acted within its discretion in finding the requested modifications to the reunification plan unreasonable.
cases.quote: We conclude that the ADA applies to the provision of reunification services

relevance.ACT-02: It establishes that a court-ordered service plan must be assessed for reasonable modifications when a parent has a disability and invokes the ADA.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification efforts that ignore a parent's disclosed disability may be legally inadequate, affecting whether reunification was genuinely attempted.
relevance.FAIL-03: It is the leading Utah authority applying a federal civil-rights statute directly to state child welfare practice.
relevance.FAIL-05: It supplies the disability-discrimination standard for challenging services and placement decisions.
relevance.PMC-01: It illustrates that federal standards are enforceable in Utah child-welfare proceedings, the doctrinal basis for federal performance oversight.

cases.holding: The Court held that whether an unwed father has acknowledged or established paternity under ICWA is governed by a federal reasonability standard rather than state law, that the birth father qualified as a 'parent' under ICWA, and that he was entitled to notice of and intervention in the adoption.
cases.quote: because he acknowledged paternity as required under ICWA, he had a right to receive notice of and to intervene in the adoption proceeding

relevance.INP-11: It is Utah's leading modern ICWA decision on who counts as a 'parent,' on federal rather than state definitions controlling, and on the rejection of the 'existing Indian family' exception.

cases.holding: The Court held that the birth mother was domiciled in Utah at the child's birth and that initiating adoption proceedings is not an 'abandonment' shifting the child's domicile to the reservation, so the state district court had jurisdiction rather than exclusive tribal jurisdiction under 25 U.S.C. § 1911(a).
cases.quote: Because a change of domicile occurs once a person establishes physical presence in a new jurisdiction with the intent to remain, we hold that C.C. was a Utah domiciliary

relevance.INP-11: It supplies the Utah test for the ICWA domicile question that decides whether a tribe has exclusive jurisdiction over a child custody proceeding.

cases.holding: The Court held that a termination petition brought under the Adoption Act in connection with a contested adoption is an 'adoption proceeding' expressly excluded from the UCCJEA, so the UCCJEA did not govern the district court's subject matter jurisdiction.
cases.quote: we conclude that the instant termination petition and related proceedings are "adoption proceedings" as defined in the UCCJEA

relevance.OUT-03: It identifies which statutory track — the Adoption Act rather than the UCCJEA — governs jurisdiction when permanency is pursued through adoption, a threshold question for any permanency placement.

cases.holding: The Court held that ICWA domicile is a matter of federal law that state abandonment doctrine cannot defeat, so the Navajo Nation had exclusive jurisdiction over the adoption of a child whose mother was domiciled on the reservation; the United States Supreme Court later adopted this reasoning in Holyfield.
cases.quote: the interests of the tribe in custodial decisions made with respect to Indian children are as entitled to respect as the interests of the parents

relevance.INP-11: It is the foundational Utah authority on ICWA's exclusive tribal jurisdiction, expressly approved by the Supreme Court in Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield.
relevance.ACT-04: It recognizes the tribe's independent interest in where an Indian child is placed, which underlies ICWA's placement preferences for extended family and tribal homes.

cases.case_name: Jensen ex rel. Jensen v. Cunningham
cases.holding: In the suit arising from the State's attempt to compel chemotherapy for a twelve-year-old, the Court held the district court wrongly applied collateral estoppel but affirmed on alternative grounds: the guardian ad litem and a testifying expert had quasi-judicial absolute immunity, and the remaining defendants' conduct was not a 'flagrant violation' of state constitutional rights.
cases.quote: the claims against the remaining three defendants fail because, as a matter of law, the facts do not demonstrate a "flagrant violation" of the Jensens' state constitutional rights

relevance.ACT-06: It is Utah's leading decision on state intervention to compel medical treatment of a child over the parents' objection and the liability consequences of that intervention.
relevance.INP-07: It arises directly from a medical provider's report and shows how a treatment dispute converts into a child welfare case.
relevance.FAIL-02: It sets the demanding 'flagrant violation' threshold and the immunities that constrain damages claims against child welfare actors under the Utah Constitution.

cases.case_name: Little v. Utah State Division of Family Services
cases.holding: The Court affirmed a judgment against the Division of Family Services for the death of an autistic child in a foster home, holding that although the decision to place a child may be discretionary, once placement occurs the agency owes and can be held to an ordinary duty of due care in supervising that placement.
cases.quote: the question was no longer whether the child was to receive foster care but whether due care was exercised under a duty assumed

relevance.ACT-03: It establishes that placing a child in foster care creates an affirmative, enforceable duty of due care in supervising that placement.
relevance.DEC-01: It marks the line between a discretionary (immune) decision and an operational duty, which is where screening and closure decisions are tested.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the Utah authority permitting recovery when a child dies from inadequate supervision of a state-arranged placement.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the leading Utah case imposing liability on the child welfare agency for a death occurring under its supervision.
relevance.PMC-04: It documents the agency-failure pattern — unheeded injury reports and inadequate follow-up — that fatality review is designed to surface.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed summary judgment for the State on the ground of duty rather than immunity, holding that corrections and supervision officials owed no duty of care to a member of the general public killed by a released offender absent a specific relationship to that individual.
cases.quote: we agree with the trial court's conclusion that no defendant had a duty of care toward the victim

relevance.DEC-01: It is the counterweight to Little: absent a specific assumed relationship to the child, the State owes no general tort duty arising from a screening or release decision.
relevance.OUT-06: It defines when a death cannot be laid at the agency's door, and so bounds Utah's fatality-liability doctrine.
relevance.FAIL-04: It requires a claimant alleging systemic failure after a death to identify a specific duty owed to the particular child, not a duty to the public generally.
relevance.PMC-04: It distinguishes a legal duty from a policy failure, which is precisely what a fatality review commission — rather than a tort suit — exists to address.

cases.case_name: Schroeder v. Utah Attorney General's Office
cases.holding: The Court held that records lawfully obtained by warrant or subpoena are not exempt from GRAMA on search-and-seizure grounds, that two documents were properly classified as attorney work product, but that disclosure was nonetheless required because the closed investigation weakened the interests favoring protection.
cases.quote: we ultimately reverse the district court's ruling because the State terminated its investigation years ago, so the interests favoring protection are not as compelling as those favoring disclosure

relevance.PMC-05: It is the operative Utah Supreme Court authority on the GRAMA balancing test a requester must satisfy to obtain protected government records.
relevance.FAIL-06: It shows that an agency's protective classification is not the end of the inquiry — courts weigh the public interest and can compel release.
relevance.INP-09: It supports outside oversight by making closed-investigation records obtainable when the public interest in accountability predominates.
relevance.PMC-02: It gives the standard for prying loose closed investigative and audit files from a state agency.
relevance.PMC-03: It supplies the legal route by which a citizen panel can obtain the underlying agency records it needs to evaluate policy.
relevance.PMC-06: It defines the balancing a requester must win before agency data can be aggregated and published.

cases.case_name: Deseret News Publishing Co. v. Salt Lake County
cases.holding: The Court held that government records are presumptively public under GRAMA and that the governmental entity bears the burden of justifying a nonpublic classification; it ordered release of an internal investigative report because the public interest in governmental accountability outweighed the asserted privacy intrusion.
cases.quote: government records are presumptively public under GRAMA, and thus, the County bears the burden of proving that it properly classified the investigative report as nonpublic

relevance.PMC-05: It places the burden of justifying secrecy on the agency, the single most useful proposition for a records requester in Utah.
relevance.FAIL-06: An agency that withholds required data must affirmatively prove its classification was proper, or the withholding is unlawful.
relevance.INP-09: It makes internal investigative reports — the raw material of oversight — presumptively obtainable.
relevance.PMC-01: It supports public access to the performance and monitoring records on which federal review depends.
relevance.PMC-02: It is the controlling authority for obtaining internal audit and investigative reports from a Utah governmental entity.
relevance.PMC-03: It gives a citizen review panel the presumption of access it needs to evaluate agency policy.
relevance.PMC-04: It supports public release of fatality and serious-injury investigative reports over privacy objections.
relevance.PMC-06: It establishes the presumption of public access that makes systematic cross-analysis of state records possible.

cases.case_name: State in the Interest of A.R.
cases.holding: The court held that the Fourth Amendment applies to a warrantless entry into a home made for child protective rather than criminal investigative purposes, but that the exclusionary rule does not bar the resulting evidence in a civil child protective proceeding, while remaining fully applicable in any related criminal case.
cases.quote: we hold that the Fourth Amendment's protection is nonetheless applicable

relevance.INP-12: It confirms that a protective-custody entry into a home is a Fourth Amendment event even when no criminal investigation is contemplated.
relevance.DEC-04: Warrantless entry incident to an emergency removal must satisfy Fourth Amendment reasonableness, not merely agency policy.
relevance.DEC-02: It governs how CPS and assisting officers may lawfully enter a home at the investigation stage.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the leading Utah appellate statement that constitutional search-and-seizure limits bind child protection workers.
relevance.INP-01: It shows the constitutional constraints that attach once a mandatory report triggers a home visit.
relevance.INP-02: A third-party report does not itself authorize a warrantless entry; the Fourth Amendment still governs.
relevance.INP-03: The entry here was by a police officer acting in a child protection role, the paradigm law-enforcement/CPS interface.
relevance.INP-06: A hotline-generated referral does not supply constitutional authority to enter a home without a warrant or exigency.
relevance.INP-07: The Fourth Amendment analysis applies equally where the referral originates from a medical or caretaking concern.
relevance.INP-10: Escalation from screening to a home investigation is the moment the Fourth Amendment attaches.
relevance.ACT-06: It confirms that evidence of a child's living conditions gathered in a protective entry is admissible in the civil proceeding authorizing care.

cases.case_name: Vigil v. Division of Child & Family Services
cases.holding: The court reversed the adjudication of domestic violence allegations because DCFS never gave Vigil notice that those allegations would be tried, while affirming the remaining rulings, including the standard of proof applied.
cases.quote: We hold that the juvenile court erred by adjudicating the domestic violence allegations against Vigil because DCFS failed to provide Vigil proper notice

relevance.DEC-03: A supported finding that feeds the DCFS Licensing System cannot rest on allegations the subject was never noticed to defend.
relevance.DEC-05: The petition defines the scope of the adjudication; allegations outside it cannot be adjudicated.
relevance.INP-04: It shows how the referral and pleading stage fixes what the court may later decide.
relevance.INP-10: Escalation to adjudication must be accompanied by notice of each allegation to be tried.
relevance.OUT-05: Allegations adjudicated without notice must be set aside, the classic ground for partial dismissal.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a clean Utah example of a court vacating an agency-driven finding for a procedural due process defect.

cases.case_name: J.J.W. v. State, Division of Child & Family Services
cases.holding: The court held that the Juvenile Expungement Statute gives the juvenile court broad authority to order DCFS to expunge its records, including entries in the non-public child abuse Database, but reversed the particular order because DCFS had no notice or opportunity to be heard.
cases.quote: the plain language of section 78-82-905 grants the juvenile court broad authority to expunge records

relevance.DEC-03: It is the Utah authority for removing a person from the DCFS abuse database, the practical remedy for a wrongful substantiated finding.
relevance.FAIL-06: It describes the statutory confidentiality regime governing the DCFS Database and who may reach it.
relevance.INP-09: It delineates the limited access rules that oversight bodies must work within when seeking DCFS records.
relevance.PMC-05: It distinguishes the non-public child abuse Database from public records, a limit any transparency effort must account for.
relevance.PMC-06: It identifies which child welfare records are statutorily closed and therefore off-limits to aggregation.

cases.holding: The court affirmed that the statutory good-faith reporter immunity of Utah Code § 62A-4a-410(1) did not protect the petitioners, because an ex parte petition for a child protective order filed with a juvenile judge is not a 'report' made to a peace officer, law enforcement agency, or DCFS.
cases.quote: An ex parte petition for a child protective order, however, does not qualify as a "report" under the statute

relevance.INP-01: It fixes the boundary of Utah's reporter immunity: the protection attaches to reports made to the statutorily designated recipients, not to court filings.
relevance.INP-02: A private person who bypasses DCFS or law enforcement and petitions a court directly forfeits the good-faith reporting immunity.
relevance.INP-06: Immunity follows the channel used: hotline or law-enforcement reports are covered, court petitions are not.
relevance.ACT-05: It is the leading Utah decision on the consequences — including fee exposure — of seeking a child protective order without merit.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the finding that further ICWA active efforts with the grandfather would be futile, but held that the State must begin complying with ICWA's placement preferences immediately after the shelter hearing and demonstrate compliance, good cause to deviate, or a concrete plan by the dispositional hearing.
cases.quote: the State must begin its attempts to comply with the ICWA's placement preferences immediately after the shelter hearing

relevance.INP-11: It is Utah's most detailed appellate treatment of ICWA active efforts and placement preferences in a dependency case.
relevance.ACT-03: It fixes the deadline — the dispositional hearing — by which a foster placement of an Indian child must be shown to comply with ICWA.
relevance.ACT-04: It requires the agency to pursue extended-family and tribal placements from the outset rather than as an afterthought.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding that DCFS's individualized modifications to the mother's service plan for her learning disabilities, agoraphobia, and domestic-violence history satisfied both the reasonable-efforts requirement and Title II of the ADA.
cases.quote: Title II of the ADA prohibits public entities from discriminating against individuals with disabilities

relevance.ACT-01: It shows what a legally adequate, disability-adapted service package looks like at the voluntary and in-home stage.
relevance.ACT-02: It applies the ADA to court-ordered service plans and describes the accommodations that make reunification efforts reasonable.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification efforts must be tailored to a parent's disclosed disability for the resulting failure to reunify to be attributed to the parent.
relevance.FAIL-03: It measures state service delivery against a federal statutory standard.
relevance.FAIL-05: It is the working Utah template for a disability-discrimination challenge to child welfare services.

cases.holding: The court affirmed, holding that the mother had been advised of and validly waived her statutory right to counsel at the adjudication hearing, that the unappealed adjudication order was separately final, and that denial of a merely statutory right to counsel requires a showing of prejudice.
cases.quote: because the right to counsel in child welfare proceedings is a statutory right, prejudice must be shown

relevance.DEC-05: It establishes that the adjudication order opening a dependency case is separately final and appealable, and that the right to counsel there is statutory rather than constitutional.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the juvenile court's substantiation of the DCFS supported finding that the mother failed to protect her child from a known sex offender, holding the finding was supported by the petition's deemed-admitted allegations and the court's own findings.
cases.quote: Because "a foundation for the court's decision exists in the evidence," this court "may not engage in a reweighing of the evidence."

relevance.DEC-03: It is the Utah model for how a DCFS supported finding is judicially substantiated and reviewed.
relevance.INP-01: It traces the path from an initial abuse report through safety planning to a judicially substantiated finding.
relevance.INP-05: It shows the legal weight given to a parent's voluntary safety-plan agreement when the parent later fails to honor it.
relevance.INP-10: It illustrates escalation from a hotline report and safety plan to a formal petition for protective supervision.
relevance.DEC-06: The safety plan was the non-court alternative first tried; its breach is what drove the case to petition.
relevance.ACT-01: It is the leading Utah illustration of the legal consequences that attach to a signed DCFS safety plan.

cases.holding: The court affirmed, holding that the juvenile court properly exercised jurisdiction where the child was found not to be an 'Indian child' (the mother's tribe being federally unrecognized) and did not abuse its discretion in declining to communicate with the tribal court, since the UCCJEA makes such communication permissive.
cases.quote: we conclude that the juvenile court properly exercised its jurisdiction and did not abuse its discretion in declining to contact the tribal court

relevance.INP-11: It addresses the threshold ICWA question — federal recognition of the tribe — and the discretionary nature of state-tribal judicial communication in Utah.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding that the juvenile court adequately considered and permissibly rejected both a kinship placement and long-term guardianship with foster families before concluding that termination was strictly necessary.
cases.quote: Whether the juvenile court correctly concluded there was no feasible alternative to terminating Mother's . . . parental rights is a mixed question of fact and law

relevance.OUT-03: It shows in detail how a juvenile court must evaluate permanent guardianship as an alternative to termination, and when rejecting it is defensible.
relevance.ACT-04: It illustrates the record a court must build when it declines an available relative placement.

cases.holding: The court affirmed a disposition order requiring a father to complete a domestic violence assessment, holding that once a child is adjudicated dependent the juvenile court has continuing jurisdiction and may impose any condition on a parent that is reasonable, proportionate, and calculated to serve the child's best interest.
cases.quote: Under section 78A-6-117(2), the juvenile court may impose conditions on a parent so long as the conditions are "reasonable."

relevance.ACT-02: It states the Utah test — reasonableness, proportionality, and connection to the child's best interest — for every court-ordered service condition.
relevance.ACT-01: It marks the boundary between voluntary participation and a judicially enforceable service condition.
relevance.ACT-05: It confirms the juvenile court's authority to impose protective conditions on a parent short of removing the child.
relevance.DEC-06: Protective supervision in the home is the least intrusive dispositional option, the court-supervised analogue to alternative response.
relevance.INP-04: It describes how adjudication establishes the jurisdiction that makes all subsequent court-ordered referrals possible.
relevance.INP-05: The dependency finding here rested on the child being without proper care through no fault of the parent, the classic voluntary-help entry point.
relevance.OUT-04: Its holding on the juvenile court's continuing jurisdiction over an adjudicated child is the nearest Utah authority to extended-jurisdiction questions for older youth.

cases.holding: The court affirmed, holding that the stepfather was not denied due process where he participated through counsel in both the shelter and adjudication hearings, and that the juvenile court could properly rely at adjudication on evidence presented during the seven-day shelter hearing given the parties' agreement.
cases.quote: we presume that those findings are supported by the evidence presented during the seven-day shelter hearing

relevance.INP-12: It shows the shelter hearing functioning as the first judicial test of an emergency protective custody decision.
relevance.DEC-04: It confirms that the evidentiary record built at the shelter hearing can carry forward and support later removal findings.
relevance.DEC-05: It addresses the procedural relationship between the shelter hearing and the adjudication on the petition.
relevance.ACT-03: It describes the hearing sequence through which a foster placement is judicially authorized and reviewed.
relevance.ACT-05: It illustrates due process protections owed to a household member subject to protective orders and findings.

cases.case_name: State, Division of Child & Family Services v. Bazzelle
cases.holding: The court denied the State's petition for extraordinary relief, holding that the juvenile court retained jurisdiction — including concurrent paternity jurisdiction — because the child welfare case remained open, and therefore did not exceed its authority.
cases.quote: Because we conclude the juvenile court did not exceed its jurisdiction, the State is ineligible for extraordinary relief.

relevance.INP-04: It confirms the breadth of the juvenile court's authority to order further inquiry and relief while a child welfare case remains open.
relevance.DEC-06: It shows that an open case, not a new petition, supplies the jurisdictional basis for continued non-removal intervention.
relevance.OUT-04: Its holding that jurisdiction persists until the child welfare case is closed is the closest Utah authority on continuing jurisdiction over a youth in care.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of both parents' rights for serious emotional abuse, rejecting their constitutional challenges, their ineffective-assistance claims, and their attacks on the findings, and upholding the determinations that DCFS made reasonable reunification efforts and that termination was strictly necessary.
cases.quote: The juvenile court's determination that termination of Parents' parental rights was strictly necessary to advance the children's best interest was supported by the record

relevance.ACT-02: It is a detailed recent illustration of what reasonable efforts and a court-ordered service plan look like in practice, including when therapy may properly be discontinued.
relevance.OUT-04: The opinion tracks older siblings who left the home at majority, and is the nearest published Utah discussion of youth transitioning out of a family under agency supervision.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding that licensure is not a prerequisite to expert qualification under Rule 702 and that the trial court acted within its discretion in admitting the psychological evaluation and the caseworker's testimony.
cases.quote: Licensing, in and of itself, is not dispositive of an expert's qualifications to offer an opinion in any given area

relevance.DEC-03: It governs the evidentiary foundation for the expert psychological opinions on which substantiated findings and termination petitions routinely rest.

cases.case_name: Malik v. Arapahoe County Department of Social Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the denial of absolute and qualified immunity, holding that it was clearly established that procuring a child-seizure order through distortion, misrepresentation, or omission violates the Fourth Amendment, and that a parent's liberty interest in familial association requires pre-deprivation process absent extraordinary circumstances.
cases.quote: except in extraordinary circumstances, a parent has a liberty interest in familial association and privacy that cannot be violated without adequate pre-deprivation procedures

relevance.FAIL-02: It is the controlling Tenth Circuit authority — binding in Utah — for § 1983 liability when a child is removed on a court order obtained by misrepresentation or omission.
relevance.DEC-04: It holds that an emergency removal requires either genuine exigency or an honestly obtained order, and that caseworkers lose absolute immunity for investigative conduct.
relevance.INP-12: It sets the constitutional floor for protective custody: pre-deprivation process unless extraordinary circumstances exist.
relevance.DEC-02: It addresses how far a caseworker may push to compel access to a child during an investigation, including where counsel has been retained.
relevance.INP-02: It shows that a report, however urgent-sounding, does not license coercive access absent legal authority.
relevance.INP-03: It involves coordinated police and social services action and the limits on that joint conduct.
relevance.INP-06: It confirms that an intake referral alone cannot justify seizure without exigency or a validly obtained order.
relevance.INP-08: It concerns attempts to obtain access to and interview a child outside the parents' presence.
relevance.INP-10: It governs the escalation from a screened-in report to compelled access to the child.
relevance.FAIL-05: It recognizes a First Amendment retaliation claim where a caseworker retaliated against a parent for retaining an attorney.

cases.case_name: Lowther v. Children Youth and Family Department
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The Tenth Circuit clarified that a threat of imminent harm is required under both the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments before officials may enter a home or seize children without a warrant or judicial authorization, while affirming qualified immunity on the claims before it.
cases.quote: even in the child welfare context, there must be a threat of imminent harm when officials enter a home or seize children without a warrant or judicial authorization

relevance.FAIL-02: It is the current, controlling Tenth Circuit statement of the exigency standard governing warrantless removals in Utah.
relevance.DEC-04: It requires imminence — not generalized risk — before an emergency removal can be made without judicial authorization.
relevance.INP-12: It fixes the constitutional threshold for taking a child into protective custody without a court order.
relevance.DEC-02: It governs warrantless entry into a home during a child abuse investigation, including the limits of consent and exigency.
relevance.INP-03: The case arises from joint law-enforcement and child welfare action and defines the shared constitutional limits on both.
relevance.INP-08: It discusses safehouse interviews of children and the constitutional constraints on that investigative step.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The Tenth Circuit affirmed qualified immunity for a caseworker who photographed portions of a child's unclothed body at school without a warrant or parental consent, holding the plaintiffs had not shown clearly established law that the special needs doctrine could not justify the search.
cases.quote: the Does have not shown that Ms. Woodard's search violated clearly established Fourth Amendment law

relevance.INP-08: It is the governing Tenth Circuit decision on searching and examining a child at school during a CPS investigation without parental consent.
relevance.DEC-02: It sets out the special needs framework — justified at inception and reasonable in scope — that measures investigative searches of children.
relevance.INP-07: It treats a quasi-medical examination of a child by a caseworker as a Fourth Amendment search subject to the special needs test.
relevance.ACT-06: It defines the constitutional limits on examining a child's body without parental consent or a warrant.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that before a State may sever the rights of parents in their natural child, due process requires proof by at least clear and convincing evidence, and that New York's fair-preponderance standard was unconstitutional.
cases.quote: We hold that such a standard adequately conveys to the factfinder the level of subjective certainty about his factual conclusions necessary to satisfy due process.

relevance.OUT-02: It is the federal constitutional floor — clear and convincing evidence — that Utah's termination statute and In re G.D. implement.
relevance.DEC-03: It establishes that the gravity of the State's allegation controls the standard of proof required before the parent-child relationship is burdened.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that there is no automatic federal constitutional right to appointed counsel in parental termination proceedings; the presumption is against appointment absent a risk of loss of physical liberty, and the question is decided case by case under Mathews v. Eldridge.
cases.quote: right to appointed counsel only when, if he loses, he may be deprived of his physical liberty

relevance.DEC-05: It explains why the right to counsel for Utah parents when a petition is filed rests on statute (Utah Code § 80-3-104) rather than on the federal Constitution.
relevance.OUT-02: It supplies the due process framework governing appointment of counsel at a termination trial.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that an unwed father was entitled as a matter of due process to a hearing on his fitness before his children could be taken from him, and that presuming all unwed fathers unfit denied equal protection.
cases.quote: We observe that the State registers no gain towards its declared goals when it separates children from the custody of fit parents.

relevance.DEC-04: It is the federal source of the rule that a child may not be taken from a parent without an individualized fitness determination.
relevance.INP-12: It requires that protective custody be justified as to the particular parent, not by categorical presumptions.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the root authority for the due process claim that arises when a child is removed without a hearing on the parent's fitness.
relevance.INP-05: It protects a parent who seeks help or comes forward voluntarily from being presumed unfit.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty on a State to protect a child from private violence, even where the agency knew of the danger, absent a custodial or other special relationship that the State itself created.
cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

relevance.DEC-01: It is the controlling federal answer to the family whose report was screened out and whose child was later harmed: no federal constitutional duty absent custody.
relevance.OUT-06: It bars most federal constitutional claims after a child dies in the home, channeling such claims into state tort law like Little and Ferree.
relevance.FAIL-04: It defines the narrow custodial exception under which a federal claim for a death under agency supervision can survive.
relevance.PMC-01: Because courts will not enforce a general protective duty, federal performance monitoring rather than litigation is the practical accountability mechanism.

cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that 'domicile' under ICWA is a matter of uniform federal law, that children born off-reservation to reservation-domiciled parents were domiciled on the reservation, and that the tribal court therefore had exclusive jurisdiction over their adoption.
cases.quote: the law of domicile Congress used in the ICWA cannot be one that permits individual reservation-domiciled tribal members to defeat the tribe's exclusive jurisdiction

relevance.INP-11: It is the controlling federal authority on ICWA's exclusive tribal jurisdiction, and it expressly adopts the Utah Supreme Court's reasoning in Halloway.
relevance.FAIL-03: It holds that state courts may not use state-law definitions to circumvent a federal child welfare mandate.

cases.case_name: Roska ex rel. Roska v. Peterson
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: On rehearing in a case arising from a Utah DCFS removal, the Tenth Circuit held that removing a child from his home with no notice, no hearing, no ex parte order and no extraordinary circumstances violated clearly established Fourteenth Amendment law, reversed the grant of qualified immunity on that claim, and held that a caseworker's reliance on a state removal statute is only one factor bearing on objective reasonableness and cannot immunize conduct the statute never authorized.
cases.quote: defendants point to no extraordinary circumstances that would justify the complete absence of pre-deprivation procedural safeguards

relevance.DEC-04: It is the Utah-arising Tenth Circuit decision holding that a decision to remove a child must be preceded by notice and a hearing, or by genuine extraordinary circumstances, and that a state removal statute providing only post-deprivation process does not supply the missing authority.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the leading wrongful-removal authority binding in Utah: the caseworkers lost qualified immunity on the Fourteenth Amendment claim because the law requiring pre-deprivation process was clearly established.
relevance.DEC-02: It marks the constitutional limit on an investigation that escalates into entry and seizure, holding the record contained no evidence from which a reasonable state actor could find exigent circumstances.
relevance.INP-08: The referral here originated with school district employees and a school nurse who took their concerns to DCFS, and the opinion traces what the agency may and may not do on that basis.
relevance.INP-01: It shows that a mandatory reporter's professional concern, even when relayed by a school nurse and treating physicians, does not by itself authorize removal without pre-deprivation process.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: In a Utah DCFS case the Tenth Circuit adopted the reasonable-suspicion standard for warrantless emergency removals — officials may remove a child without prior notice and a hearing when they reasonably suspect an immediate threat to the child's safety if she remains, and must still provide a prompt post-removal hearing — but affirmed qualified immunity because that standard was not clearly established when these defendants acted.
cases.quote: In our view, the reasonable suspicion standard appropriately balances the interests of the parents, the child, and the state.

relevance.DEC-04: It supplies the Tenth Circuit's operative test for an emergency removal decision — reasonable suspicion of an immediate threat, judged on all relevant circumstances — and is the framework Lowther later revisits.
relevance.INP-12: It fixes what protective custody without a court order requires in Utah and confirms that a prompt post-removal hearing is owed even when the emergency removal was justified.
relevance.INP-01: The case began with a pediatrician's report of a child's injury to DCFS, and the court measures what that mandatory report could and could not justify.
relevance.INP-07: It is the Tenth Circuit's fullest treatment of a removal driven by a medical disclosure, including the significance of the treating physician's own view of immediacy.

cases.holding: The Court held that the court of appeals used the wrong standard when it reversed a juvenile court's finding that an infant was abused and neglected in his father's care, and remanded for review under rule 52(a)'s clearly-erroneous standard, under which findings may be set aside only if they are against the clear weight of the evidence or leave the reviewing court with a firm and definite conviction that a mistake was made.
cases.quote: The result must be against the clear weight of the evidence or leave the appellate court with a firm and definite conviction that a mistake has been made.

relevance.FAIL-01: It is the Utah Supreme Court's statement of how much is required before an appellate court may set aside a juvenile court's findings, and is the predicate on which State ex rel. B.R. and In re E.R. rest.
relevance.DEC-03: It governs review of an abuse-and-neglect adjudication, holding that a heightened standard of proof below makes it easier, but never automatic, to show the finding was clearly erroneous.
relevance.OUT-05: It explains that an appellate court may not undo an adjudication merely because it is convinced the evidence was inadequate; the result must offend the clear weight of the evidence.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed, holding that the juvenile court had subject matter jurisdiction because the mother voluntarily placed K.F. in state custody, that the order ending reunification and setting a goal of individualized permanency was final and appealable and appropriate where compelling reasons ruled out reunification, adoption, guardianship and kinship placement, and that the juvenile court's findings on service-plan compliance and on DCFS's reasonable efforts were owed broad discretion and were not clearly in error.
cases.quote: appellate courts defer to juvenile courts on matters of credibility, and juvenile courts have broad discretion in determining whether reasonable reunification efforts were made

relevance.ACT-02: It is the Utah Supreme Court authority on court-ordered service plans and the deference owed a juvenile court's finding that DCFS's efforts under that plan were reasonable.
relevance.OUT-01: It holds that whether reunification efforts were reasonable is a fact-intensive judgment for the juvenile court, and that a permanency goal may be moved off reunification when the parent has not complied with the service plan.
relevance.OUT-03: Individualized permanency is available only where there is a compelling reason to rule out reunification, adoption, guardianship and kinship placement, so this case defines the outer boundary of the guardianship and kinship track.
relevance.OUT-04: Its approval of long-term, potentially permanent foster care as a permanency goal is the closest Utah Supreme Court authority to the position of a youth who will remain in care rather than exit to a family.
relevance.DEC-06: It shows the juvenile court deploying protective supervision services in the home before any change of custody, and confirms the court's continuing authority over that non-removal disposition.
relevance.INP-04: It describes the jurisdictional predicate for every later court-ordered referral and service in a dependency case.
relevance.INP-05: It holds that a parent who voluntarily places a child in state custody thereby supplies the juvenile court's jurisdiction, the central legal consequence of a guardian's request for help.

cases.holding: The Court reversed summary judgment in a libel action, holding that the good-faith immunity of Utah's child abuse reporting statute attaches only to a report made to the nearest peace officer, law enforcement agency, or the Division, so a social worker's letters to a city mayor, to opposing counsel and to a court commissioner were not immunized reports and were not protected by the judicial-proceeding privilege either.
cases.quote: Its purpose is certainly not to require, much less immunize, the general dissemination of allegations of child abuse, one of the most defamatory charges that can be made against anyone.

relevance.INP-01: It is the foundational Utah Supreme Court decision fixing the boundary of reporter immunity: the protection runs to reports channelled to the statutory recipients, not to communications broadcast elsewhere.
relevance.INP-02: A private or third-party communication alleging abuse that bypasses law enforcement and the Division forfeits the statutory good-faith immunity, whatever the reporter's sincerity.
relevance.INP-06: It confirms that immunity follows the reporting channel, which is the legal reason hotline and law-enforcement reports are protected and other disclosures are not.
relevance.INP-07: The reporter was a hospital clinical social worker acting on a medical referral, so the case defines how far a health-care provider's abuse conclusion may travel before immunity is lost.

cases.holding: The court disavowed its 'almost automatically' line of cases, held that the statutory 'strictly necessary' requirement is analyzed as part of the best-interest element rather than as a separate third element, held that best interest must therefore be applied more thoroughly and independently than earlier cases suggested, and remanded for reconsideration — the decision the Utah Supreme Court affirmed in 2020.
cases.quote: we conclude that courts should analyze the "strictly necessary" language as part of the "best interest" element of our historical test

relevance.OUT-02: It is the working exposition of Utah's termination test that practitioners cite alongside the Supreme Court's affirmance, and it is the decision that ended the inference that statutory grounds carry best interest almost automatically.
relevance.OUT-03: By requiring an independent best-interest analysis rather than an inference from grounds, it is the decision that obliges a juvenile court to weigh guardianship and other permanency options short of termination.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding that the juvenile court is presumed to have applied the clear-and-convincing standard absent record evidence to the contrary, that the State made out a prima facie case of reasonable efforts, and that the court did not abuse its discretion in determining after trial that DCFS had made reasonable reunification efforts.
cases.quote: we discern no abuse of the juvenile court's discretion in its ultimate determination, made as factfinder after trial, that DCFS provided reasonable efforts toward reunification

relevance.ACT-02: It is the current Utah statement of how a reasonable-efforts determination on a court-ordered service plan is reviewed, and of what a parent must show to upset one.
relevance.OUT-01: It holds that friction with a caseworker and delay in starting family therapy did not make the reunification effort unreasonable, defining how much shortfall a parent must prove before the failure to reunify can be laid at the agency's door.

cases.holding: The Court reversed, holding that a mother's fundamental parental rights were severed when the district court terminated them for failing to strictly comply with the Adoption Act's intervention procedures, and that the strict-compliance provision of Utah Code section 78B-6-110 failed strict scrutiny and was unconstitutional as applied to her because her timely, substantially compliant motion achieved everything the provision exists to achieve.
cases.quote: because the strict compliance requirement did not further the State's compelling, adoption-related interests in this case, we hold that the strict compliance requirement is unconstitutional as applied in this case

relevance.DEC-05: It is the modern Utah Supreme Court authority on what process is due a parent at the pleading stage: a procedural default rule may not be applied to sever parental rights unless doing so actually serves a compelling state interest.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a recent example of the Utah Supreme Court reversing a lower court for a constitutional defect in how a parent's rights were terminated, and it supplies the standard of review for such constitutional claims.

notes: Every case listed was retrieved from CourtListener in this session (search API plus /opinions/<id>/ full text) and each quote was programmatically verified as an exact substring of the retrieved opinion text after whitespace/quote-mark normalization. No case or quote was taken from memory.

I have given the citation the Utah Supreme Court uses. Counsel should confirm against the official reporter; CourtListener's cluster metadata appears to preserve an early slip designation.

Parallel P.3d citations for In re A.H. (554 P.3d 969), In re E.R. (496 P.3d 58) and In re G.D. (491 P.3d 867) were taken from the text of other Utah Supreme Court opinions retrieved in this session (In re D.S., 2025 UT 11; In re J.P., 2021 UT App 134), because the CourtListener clusters carry only the Utah public-domain citation. Utah's public-domain citation (e.g. '2022 UT 39', '2021 UT App 134') is the official citation form in Utah, so entries without a P.3d parallel are complete.

CourtListener holds multiple duplicate clusters for several Utah cases (e.g. N.D. v. State / In re K.C., 2015 UT 92 appears as clusters 6655725, 5345104, 3163192 and 3158054). I selected the cluster whose record carries the full reporter citation and whose opinion text was retrievable; a lawyer following a link may encounter the duplicates.

Several Utah Court of Appeals entries are per curiam 'Decision' documents rather than full signed opinions (A.G. v. State, 2014 UT App 22; K.C. v. State, 2017 UT App 94; S.A. v. State, 2016 UT App 191). These are not unpublished memoranda - each is published in the Pacific Reporter and is citable Utah precedent - but they are short and fact-bound, and they are used here only for the narrow propositions quoted. Where a signed published opinion existed on the same point I preferred it.

In re Adoption of B.B., 2017 UT 59 (cluster 4423655) is a fractured decision in which different majorities formed on different issues; the quoted passage comes from Justice Himonas's opinion designated 'Opinion of the Court in part' and from the disposition that commanded a majority (reversal of the denial of the birth father's motion to intervene). Counsel should read the alignment of the justices before relying on any other portion.

Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000) was retrieved and read but is NOT included: the 'presumption that fit parents act in the best interests of their children' appears in a plurality opinion, not a majority opinion, and the instructions bar quoting from a non-majority writing. Utah's own fit-parent presumption authority should be sought in the state statutes and in In re B.T.B.

OUT-04 (Extended Foster Care / Aging Out) has NO on-point Utah appellate authority. Targeted searches of the Utah Supreme Court and Court of Appeals for extended foster care, care to age 21, Chafee independent-living services, and jurisdiction past age 18 returned nothing construing those programs. The cases mapped to OUT-04 address the juvenile court's continuing jurisdiction over an adjudicated child (S.A. v. State; State DCFS v. Bazzelle), long-term potentially permanent foster care as a permanency goal (In re K.F.), and youth leaving a supervised household at majority (In re H.H.); they are the nearest available authority, and the governing law for this node remains the federal Chafee Foster Care Independence Act (Pub. L. 106-169) and Fostering Connections (Pub. L. 110-351) as implemented by Utah Code Title 80, Chapter 2, Part 3.

FAIL-03 (Federal Compliance Failure) and PMC-01 through PMC-04 have no Utah appellate case law. No reported Utah decision adjudicates CFSR performance, Title IV-E penalty exposure, Single Audit Act findings, CAPTA Citizen Review Panels, or the Protect Our Kids Act. The cases mapped to those nodes are the closest functional authority: N.D. v. State and A.W. v. State (federal statutory standards are enforceable against Utah child welfare practice), Holyfield (state law cannot be used to evade a federal child welfare mandate), DeShaney (no judicially enforceable protective duty, so oversight rather than litigation is the accountability route), and the GRAMA and tort cases that supply the records-access and fatality-accountability mechanisms. The operative law for these nodes is federal: 42 U.S.C. Sec. 5106a(c), 45 C.F.R. Part 1355, and 31 U.S.C. Sec. 7501 et seq.

PMC-06 (Project Milk Carton AI Analysis) is an analytic node with no possible case law of its own; it is mapped to the Utah records-access authorities (Deseret News, Schroeder, J.J.W.) that determine what state data may lawfully be obtained and republished. Note the hard limit J.J.W. identifies: the DCFS child abuse Database is statutorily non-public and is not reachable through GRAMA.

No published Utah appellate decision was found on children who go missing from foster care, on child-fatality review commission practice, or on sibling-placement rights as an independent claim. Searches for each returned either nothing or only fact-bound memoranda; those topics are therefore covered only indirectly (Little and Ferree for fatality/serious injury; In re J.P. and In re G.D. for placement alternatives).

Practice point for FAIL-02: Utah sits in the Tenth Circuit, so Malik (1999), Roska (2003), Gomes (2006) and Lowther (2024) - not state law - supply the operative Fourth/Fourteenth Amendment standard for wrongful-removal Section 1983 claims. Read in sequence: Malik establishes the pre-deprivation-process rule and liability for orders procured by misrepresentation; Roska applies it to a Utah DCFS removal and strips qualified immunity; Gomes adopts the reasonable-suspicion test for warrantless emergency removals; Lowther clarifies that imminent harm is required under both amendments. Note that State in the Interest of A.R. holds the exclusionary rule does NOT suppress unlawfully obtained evidence in the civil child protective proceeding itself, so a Fourth Amendment violation in Utah is remedied in damages, not by suppression.

Practice point for DEC-03: Utah's substantiation architecture runs through the juvenile court (K.C. v. State), the notice requirement (Vigil), and the expungement remedy for the DCFS Database (J.J.W.). In re A.B. (2022 UT 39) is the current Utah Supreme Court authority that a neglect finding must match the statutory definition and that this is reviewed nondeferentially as a law-like mixed question; State ex rel. Z.D. (2006 UT 54) supplies the clear-error standard that governs the underlying factual findings.
Budget: 126 CourtListener API requests were used in the prior pass, within the 150-request limit and the one-request-per-two-seconds pacing. Justia was not fetched.

Opinion text retrieved and read; the quote is from Chief Judge Tacha's opinion for the panel. Note this is the April 29, 2003 revised opinion on rehearing, which withdrew and replaced the September 5, 2002 opinion reported at 304 F.3d 982 (cluster 162558) - cite the 2003 version.

Wood, 451 F.3d 1122 (10th Cir. 2006) (cluster 167696) for DEC-04, INP-12, INP-01 and INP-07: it adopts the reasonable-suspicion standard for warrantless emergency removals in a Utah DCFS case and holds that a prompt post-removal hearing is owed even when the emergency removal was justified. Lowther cannot be read accurately without it, as Lowther expressly revisits this framework.

Added State ex rel. Z.D., 2006 UT 54, 147 P.3d 401 (cluster 2621342) for FAIL-01, DEC-03 and OUT-05: it is the Utah Supreme Court's rule 52(a) clear-error decision, the predicate for State ex rel. B.R. and In re E.R., and it supplies the measure of how far an appellate court's discomfort with juvenile court findings must go before intercession is permitted. CourtListener also carries this decision as cluster 5324416 ('S.B.D. v. State'); the same opinion text is at both.

Added In re K.F., 2009 UT 4, 201 P.3d 985 (cluster 2634909) for ACT-02, OUT-01, OUT-03, OUT-04, DEC-06, INP-04 and INP-05: it is the Utah Supreme Court authority on juvenile court jurisdiction arising from a voluntary placement, on the finality of an order changing a permanency goal, on individualized permanency as a permanency option, and on the broad discretion owed a reasonable-efforts determination. It replaces the per curiam S.A. v. State as the primary anchor at several of these nodes (S.A. is retained).

Added Allen v. Ortez, 802 P.2d 1307 (Utah 1990) (cluster 1351415) for INP-01, INP-02, INP-06 and INP-07: it is the Utah Supreme Court decision defining the outer boundary of the good-faith child-abuse reporter immunity - letters to a mayor, to opposing counsel and to a court commissioner are not 'reports' under the statute - and it is the foundation Cammack-White later applies. It rescues INP-01, INP-02 and INP-06, each of which previously carried a single case.

Practitioners cite the two together. The CourtListener cluster carries only the Utah public-domain citation.

NOTE: the CourtListener cluster carries only '2023 UT App 27' and no P.3d parallel, so the reported parallel citation 527 P.3d 1114 could NOT be verified from CourtListener in this session and is therefore omitted from the citation field; the Utah public-domain citation is the official form and is complete without it.

The quoted passage is from Chief Justice Durrant's opinion of the Court, joined by Justices Himonas and Pearce (Justice Petersen concurring in the result; Associate Chief Justice Lee dissenting) - do not rely on the dissent or the separate concurrence. (4786137) was unmapped in the prior node_map despite carrying an OUT-03 relevance sentence, and has been added to OUT-03. Each case's relevance object may therefore list a node that the trimmed node_map no longer carries; the relevance text remains accurate as a statement of what the case says.

Nodes that previously carried fewer than two cases - INP-01, INP-02, INP-07, INP-08 and DEC-06 - now carry four to six. INP-01/02/06 were filled by Allen v. Ortez (Utah Supreme Court, the leading published authority on the point); INP-07 by Allen v. Ortez and Gomes v. Wood; DEC-06 by In re K.F. plus the existing S.A. v. State and Bazzelle. INP-08 (Educational Disclosure) has NO Utah appellate authority: a targeted Utah Supreme Court and Court of Appeals search for mandatory-reporter, school-teacher and school-nurse reporting returned zero published results, and a search for caseworker interviews of children at school without parental consent returned only State in the Interest of A.R. and one 2025 memorandum. The governing law at INP-08 is therefore Tenth Circuit: Doe v. Woodard (search/examination of a child at school under the special needs doctrine), Malik (access to a child outside the parents' presence) and Roska (school-originated referral to DCFS), plus Lowther on safehouse interviews.

DEC-06 (Differential Response / Alternative Response) has no Utah appellate decision construing a formal differential-response or alternative-response track. Searches of both Utah appellate courts for in-home services short of a petition returned only cases about protective supervision as a court-ordered disposition. The four cases mapped there are the nearest Utah analogues - the voluntary safety plan (K.C. v. State), protective supervision services in the home before any custody change (In re K.F.), protective supervision as the least intrusive disposition (S.A. v. State), and continued non-removal intervention under an already-open case (Bazzelle). The operative law for a true differential-response track remains federal (FFPSA, Title IV-B/IV-E prevention funding) as implemented by Utah Code Title 80.

Caveat on A.D.T. v. State (In re C.D.), 2008 UT App 477 (cluster 5325594): the Utah Supreme Court granted certiorari and then, in Guardian Ad Litem v. State ex rel. C.D., 2010 UT 66, 245 P.3d 724 (cluster 2366063, retrieved and read in this session), dismissed the petitions as moot because the children had been placed with their biological fathers, declining to reach the ICWA active-efforts and placement-preference issues and declining to vacate the court of appeals opinion. The Supreme Court expressed neither approval nor disapproval of the court of appeals decision, so A.D.T. remains citable Court of Appeals precedent, but counsel should disclose this history.

Distinct case count is now 50, above the 20-40 target range. This is the consequence of a gap-closing pass that had to leave the reconciled brief's 42 existing entries unchanged while adding eight leading authorities the verifier identified as missing. Every node still sits within the 2-6 case ceiling.
Budget for this pass: 25 CourtListener API requests (search, cluster and opinion endpoints), paced at one request per two seconds. No request failed and no 429 was returned. Justia was not fetched.
All eight authorities named by the verifier were found, retrieved, read and included. There is no authority on that list that could not be verified.

Missing (for a later pass): In re J.P., 648 P.2d 1364 (Utah 1982) — verified on CourtListener (cluster 5327821, Utah Sup. Ct., June 9, 1982). This is the most conspicuous gap in the brief. It is Utah's foundational constitutional decision on termination of parental rights, holding that parental rights are fundamental and that a statute permitting termination on a bare 'best interest' showing, without unfitness, abandonment or substantial neglect, cannot stand. Every OUT-02 authority in the brief — B.T.B., A.H., G.D., D.S. — builds on it, and the Utah Supreme Court still cites it as the source of the state constitutional dimension of parental rights. Its absence leaves OUT-02 and DEC-05 resting entirely on the modern statutory-gloss cases with no Utah constitutional anchor, and it is also the authority a practitioner would reach for in place of the Troxel plurality the brief correctly declined to quote.

Missing (for a later pass): Yvonne L. v. New Mexico Department of Human Services, 959 F.2d 883 (10th Cir. 1992) — verified on CourtListener (clusters 580032 and 9006488). This is the Tenth Circuit's leading statement that children placed in state custody have a substantive due process right to reasonably safe conditions, and that officials are liable where the placement decision represents a failure to exercise professional judgment. It is the affirmative side of the DeShaney custodial exception and is binding in Utah. FAIL-04 and OUT-06 currently cite DeShaney for the bar without citing the circuit authority that defines the exception a foster-care claimant would actually plead, which makes those nodes read far more pessimistically than the law supports.

Missing (for a later pass): Schwartz v. Booker, 702 F.3d 573 (10th Cir. 2012) — verified on CourtListener (cluster 813921). The modern Tenth Circuit application of the special-relationship doctrine to the death of a child in foster care, holding that caseworkers who placed and then failed to monitor the child were not entitled to qualified immunity. It is the case a practitioner would pair with Yvonne L. at FAIL-04 and OUT-06, and it post-dates every fatality authority the brief carries (Little, 1983; Ferree, 1989; DeShaney, 1989). Without it the brief's fatality nodes rest on two 1980s Utah tort cases and a federal no-duty rule.

Missing (for a later pass): Dubbs ex rel. Dubbs v. Head Start, Inc., 336 F.3d 1194 (10th Cir. 2003) — verified on CourtListener (cluster 163684). The Tenth Circuit's authority on invasive physical examinations of children conducted without parental notice or consent, holding such examinations are Fourth Amendment searches and rejecting a categorical special-needs justification. It is the natural companion to Doe v. Woodard at INP-08 and DEC-02, and it is the authority ACT-06 actually needs: that node presently has only Jensen genuinely on point, with Doe v. Woodard padding it. Dubbs cuts the other way from Woodard on the special-needs question and a brief citing Woodard alone misstates the state of the law.

Missing (for a later pass): Bolden v. Doe (In re Adoption of J.S.), 2014 UT 51, 358 P.3d 1009 — verified on CourtListener (clusters 2748023, 2747938, 2754059). The Utah Supreme Court's major modern decision on the rights of an unmarried biological father under the Adoption Act and the constitutional status of an inchoate parental interest. It is the doctrinal predecessor to In re Adoption of K.T.B. (2020 UT 51), which the brief does include, and it is what a practitioner would cite at DEC-05 and OUT-02 for the proposition that the Act's procedural preconditions are measured against the father's constitutionally protected interest. Note the decision is fractured with a dissent by Justice Parrish, so any quotation must be checked against the alignment.

Missing (for a later pass): Salt Lake City Corp. v. Jordan River Restoration Network, 2018 UT 62, 435 P.3d 179 — verified on CourtListener (cluster 4576258, Petersen, J., opinion of the Court). The Utah Supreme Court's controlling modern decision on how a GRAMA request must be framed and how a governmental entity must respond to a broad request. PMC-05, PMC-02, PMC-03 and PMC-06 all rest on Deseret News (2008) and Schroeder (2015) for the presumption and the balancing test, but neither tells a requester what a legally sufficient request looks like or what the entity's obligations are in responding — which is the first practical question in any transparency effort and the ground on which such requests are most often defeated.
